entries.modern_form: PIE *(s)kewh₁- 'to perceive, observe, pay attention' (Pokorny 1. keu-, skeu-, lengthened kēu- p.587; Watkins keu-¹ / keuə-¹)
entries.note: Pokorny IEW p.587 heads the entry '1. keu-, skeu-, dehnstufig kēu- „worauf achten (beobachten, schauen)“, dann „hören, fühlen, merken“; schwere Basis keuə-; s-Erweiterung keu-s-; … d-Erweiterung keud- : kūd- in keudos : kūdos „Ruhm“' — so Nourai's four headword shapes are exactly the variants his source lists: Keu = keu-, Kou = the o-grade *kou- of *kouos (whence Gk. koéō, Lat. caveō), Skeu/Skou = the s-mobile variants (§'2. Mit anlautendem s-', p.588). Language label 'Indo-European' and gloss 'to watch, see, hear' both reproduce Pokorny faithfully. Modern handbooks write the root *(s)kewh₁- 'to perceive'. Two caveats the chart does not show: (a) Walde-Pokorny I 370 itself warns that the s-initial group is semantically restricted to seeing and that 'ihre Verwandtschaft mit qeu- „worauf achten, merken“ ganz fraglich' ist — i.e. Nourai's merging of Skeu with Keu is the traditional but not uncontested arrangement; (b) Watkins/AHD splits what Nourai unites into keu-¹ ('to perceive, see, hear': hear, show, acoustic) and keuə-¹ ('to pay attention': cavēre, kudos), the two halves that feed Nourai's Latin/Greek and Germanic branches respectively. Beekes (per Wiktionary s.v. κῦδος) rejects the derivation of kudos from this root altogether, positing *kewd-s- 'miraculous power'.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپاییِ آغازینِ *(s)kewh₁- به معنی «نگریستن، دریافتن، شنیدن» است. پوکورنی در صفحهٔ ۵۸۷ فرهنگ خود سرواژه را چنین آورده است: «keu-، skeu-، و با کشیدگی kēu-: توجه کردن (نگریستن)، سپس شنیدن، احساس کردن، دریافتن»؛ پس هر چهار صورتی که نورایی نوشته (Keu، Kou، Skeu، Skou) همان گونه‌های آوایی‌اند که منبعش برشمرده است: Kou صورت o-دار *kouos است که لاتینی caveō و یونانی koéō از آن برآمده، و Skeu/Skou همان گونهٔ دارای «سِ متحرک» (s-mobile) است. برچسب زبانی و معنای داده‌شده هر دو درست‌اند. تنها دو نکته: نخست آنکه والده-پوکورنی (جلد ۱، ص ۳۷۰) خودْ پیوند گونه‌های s-دار را با keu- «مشکوک» می‌خواند؛ دوم آنکه واتکینز این خانواده را به دو ریشهٔ جداگانه (keu-¹ و keuə-¹) بخش کرده است. در مجموع ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ خودِ ریشه درست است.

nodes.derivation: Avestan kauui- (stem kavay-, Bartholomae AiW col. 442-443 '*kavay- m.') is the direct Iranian continuation of PIE *(s)kewh₁-i- 'one who perceives' (= Skt. kaví-), through Proto-Indo-Iranian *káwHiš; PIE *ḱ/*k before the front vowel gives Indo-Iranian k, and the -i- stem is unchanged. Its Avestan sense is 'poet-priest, seer, vision-poet' in the Gāthās (where kauui- are often opponents of Zaraθuštra) and dynastic 'prince/ruler' in the Younger Avesta, where the Kauui line runs Kauui Kauuāta, Kauui Usan, Kauui Haosrauuah, Kauui Vīštāspa (Yt.13.132-133, Yt.19.71). 'kâvâ-usân' renders the attested nominative kauua usa (Yt.5.45) / genitive kauuōis usaδanō (Yt.13.133) = 'Kavi Usan'. Two reservations: (a) Nourai's gloss 'sovereign' for kavi is the later, Sasanian reinterpretation — Wiktionary, following Skjærvø, notes that 'the visionary poets of the Avesta were mistakenly interpreted as ancient kings by the Sasanian Zoroastrian priests'; (b) 'rich king' for kāvā-usān is a folk gloss: usan-/usaδan- is a proper name (Bartholomae: 'usaδan- m. EN. zweier Gläubiger … eines iranischen Fürsten, der auch usan- heisst'), cognate with Vedic Uśanas Kāvya, not a word for 'rich'.
nodes.derivation_fa: واژهٔ اوستایی kauui- (ستاک kavay-) دنبالهٔ مستقیم *káwHiš ایرانی باستان و آن از ریشهٔ هندواروپایی *(s)kewh₁- است و با kaví- سنسکریت یکی است. معنای آن در گاهان «شاعرِ بینا، پیشوای دینیِ نامزرتشتی» و در اوستای نو عنوان دودمان کیانی است (کَوی کَواتَ، کَوی اوسَن، کَوی هَئوسرَوَه، کَوی ویشتاسپ). دو نکته: نخست آنکه معنی «پادشاه» که نورایی داده تعبیر متأخر روزگار ساسانی است، نه معنای اصلی اوستایی؛ دوم آنکه ترجمهٔ «پادشاه توانگر» برای kāvā-usān ریشه‌شناسی عامیانه است، زیرا usan-/usaδan- نام خاص است (بارتولومه، ستون ۴۰۶ و ذیل usaδan-) و هم‌ریشه با اوشَنَس کاویه در ودا، نه واژه‌ای به معنی «توانگر». پس ادعای نورایی در اصلِ اشتقاق درست ولی در معنا با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian kay (Book Pahlavi <kd>, on coins kd/kdy) continues Old Iranian *kavi- with the regular loss of the Old Iranian -i stem-vowel and monophthongisation of the resulting *kavi > kay; it survives only as the dynastic title of the Kayanians (the line of Kay Kawād, Kay Us, Kay Husraw, Kay Wištāsp), with the oblique plural kayān 'the Kayanids'. 'kayos' is MP Kāyōs / Kay-Us [k'dws], the compound of kay with the name of the second Kayanid, Av. Kauui Usan (gen. usaδanō): Av. usan- > MP -ōs by the usual Middle Persian raising of Old Iranian a before a nasal-final syllable and loss of the final -n. Nyberg's glossary gives exactly this equation. As at node 1, the gloss 'rich king' for kayos has no support: Usan is a name, and Nyberg, MacKenzie and the Pahlavi Bundahišn treat Kāyōs simply as a personal name. MacKenzie's dictionary also warns that the ideographic spelling <kd> makes kay 'when?' and kay 'Kayanian' homographs.
nodes.derivation_fa: «کی» فارسی میانه (پهلوی <kd>، بر سکه‌ها kd/kdy) دنبالهٔ *kavi- ایرانی باستان است؛ افتادن واکهٔ پایانی و تک‌واکه‌شدن *kavi به kay دگرگونی آوایی منظم فارسی میانه است. این واژه در پهلوی تنها به‌صورت لقب دودمانی به‌کار می‌رود (کی‌کواد، کی‌اوس، کی‌هوسرَو، کی‌ویشتاسپ) و جمع مضاف‌الیهی آن kayān است. «kayos» همان Kāyōs (کی‌اوس) پهلوی است، مرکب از kay و نام دومین شهریار کیانی، اوستایی Kauui Usan؛ نیبرگ در واژه‌نامهٔ خود به‌روشنی می‌نویسد: «Kāyōs … Av. (406) kavi- usan-, nom. kava usa». باز هم ترجمهٔ «پادشاه توانگر» درست نیست، چون Usan نام خاص است. بنابراین اشتقاق نورایی پذیرفتنی است ولی معنایی که برای جزء دوم آورده تأیید نمی‌شود.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian qwy /kaw/ (Manichaean, Christian and Sogdian-script texts; oblique/plural kwʾyst 'giants') is the same Old Iranian *kavi- continued in the north-eastern branch, where the -i- stem was lost and the diphthong preserved as -aw. The semantic shift 'Kavi > giant, hero' is Manichaean: in the Sogdian and Middle Persian versions of Mani's Book of Giants the antediluvian giants are called kawān/kawi, because the Iranian translators equated the Enochic giants with the pre-Zoroastrian Kavis of Iranian legend (Henning, 'The Book of the Giants', BSOAS 11, 1943, pp. 52-74, esp. pp. 53, 68, 70 — cited in Gharib's entry). Parthian shows the same word and sense (Nyberg: 'MPrth kw, pl. cas. obl. qʾwʾn „giant“'). Strictly the arrow should read 'Old Iranian *kavi-' rather than 'Avestan', since Sogdian does not descend from Avestan; Gharib's own note '<Av. kavi' uses the Avestan form as the standard citation shape, exactly as Nourai does.
nodes.derivation_fa: واژهٔ سغدی qwy (خوانش kaw، جمع kwʾyst «غولان») همان *kavi- ایرانی باستان است که در شاخهٔ شمال‌شرقی ایرانی، با افتادن واکهٔ ستاکی و نگاه‌داشت دوواکهٔ -aw، به این صورت رسیده است. تحول معنایی «کَوی ← غول، پهلوان» زادهٔ ادبیات مانوی است: در ترجمهٔ سغدی و پارسی میانهٔ «کتاب غولان» مانی، غولانِ پیش از طوفان kawān خوانده شده‌اند، زیرا مترجمان ایرانی آنان را با کَویانِ پیش‌زرتشتی یکی گرفتند (هنینگ، BSOAS ۱۱، ص ۵۳ و ۷۰). در پارتی نیز همین واژه با همین معنا هست (نیبرگ: qʾwʾn «غول»). تنها نکتهٔ دقیق آن است که سغدی از اوستایی نمی‌آید، بلکه هر دو از ایرانی باستان‌اند؛ قریب هم صورت اوستایی را تنها به‌عنوان صورت شاهد آورده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: New Persian کی kay 'king (of the Kayanian line)' continues MP kay unchanged; the compounds کیقباد، کیخسرو، کیکاووس that Nourai adds beside it are the Šāhnāma forms of MP Kay-Kawād, Kay-Husraw, Kay-Kāwus. کاووس Kāvus is MP Kāyōs/Kay-Us with the Persian spelling -او- for the long ō; its Arabised doublet قابوس Qābūs (Nourai's parenthesis) is the same name taken into Arabic with the regular substitution of q- for k- and ب for the Persian -w- (the Ziyarid Qābūs b. Wušmgīr). کیان kayān is the inherited Middle Persian oblique plural of kay, reused in New Persian as an ordinary plural 'kings', whence the adjective کیانی 'Kayanian'; کیانوش is a Šāhnāma proper name built on the same element. کیا kiyā, a Caspian title ('a great man, a lord, a margrave' — Mo'in), is the same word with the -ā of the vocative/emphatic; it is the title of the Kiā dynasty of Gilān and of the Zaydī sayyids of Ṭabaristān. Mo'in's footnote in Borhān records a competing view for the Kurdish form (Jaba deriving Kurdish kia from Persian کدخدا), but keeps کیا itself under کی.
nodes.derivation_fa: «کی» فارسی نو دنبالهٔ بی‌تغییر kay پهلوی است و ترکیب‌های کیقباد، کیخسرو و کیکاووس همان Kay-Kawād و Kay-Husraw و Kay-Kāwus پهلوی‌اند. «کاووس» صورت فارسیِ Kāyōs پهلوی است که در آن ō کشیده به «او» نوشته شده؛ «قابوس» معرّب همان نام است (ابدال ک به ق و و به ب، مانند نام قابوس بن وشمگیر زیاری). «کیان» جمعِ مضاف‌الیهیِ به‌ارث‌ماندهٔ پهلوی است که در فارسی نو جمع عادی «پادشاهان» شده و صفت «کیانی» از آن ساخته شده است. «کیا» عنوانی مازندرانی–گیلانی است به معنی «بزرگ ناحیه، پادشاه کوچک، مرزبان» (معین) و از همین ریشه است. برهان قاطع به تصحیح معین در صفحات ۱۷۴۹–۱۷۵۱ همهٔ این واژه‌ها را زیر «کی» و «کیا» و «کیان» آورده و در حاشیه به اوستایی kavi بازگردانده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Persian شکوه šokuh/šukōh 'glory, majesty, grandeur' goes back to Middle Persian škōh (Book Pahlavi <škwh>, Manichaean MP ʾyšqwhʾn) from Old Iranian *skauaθa-, a -θa- abstract to the s-mobile form *skau- 'to look at' of this very root: the formation is exactly parallel to MP handōh > NP اندوه andōh 'sorrow' from *san-day-aθa-, as Bartholomae showed. The semantic path is 'what is looked at' > 'imposing appearance, dignity' > 'splendour, majesty' — Bartholomae compares German schön and Ansehen, and Pokorny prints the equation verbatim. Initial *sk- gives Middle Persian š(k)-, and prothetic i-/e- appears in the Manichaean spelling ʾyšqwh-. Modern Persian has the doublets شکوه šokuh and شکوه šekuh/شکوهیدن; the homophone شکوه 'complaint' is a separate Arabic loan (شَكْوَة šakwa) and is not involved here. Nourai attaches the node directly to the root, which is right, since the s-form does not pass through the Avestan kavi- branch.
nodes.derivation_fa: «شُکوه» فارسی از فارسی میانهٔ škōh (پهلویِ کتابی <škwh>، مانوی ʾyšqwhʾn) و آن از ایرانی باستان *skauaθa- است، یعنی اسم‌مصدری با پسوند -aθa- از گونهٔ s-دارِ همین ریشه (*skau- «نگریستن»). بارتولومه این ساخت را دقیقاً با «اندوه» سنجیده است: andōh < handōh < *san-day-aθa-. تحول معنایی چنین بوده است: «آنچه دیده می‌شود» ← «هیبت و آبرو» ← «شکوه و بزرگی»؛ خودِ بارتولومه واژهٔ آلمانی schön و Ansehen را برای همین دگرگونی معنایی شاهد می‌آورد. خوشهٔ آغازینِ *sk- در فارسی میانه به š(k)- بدل شده و در نگارش مانوی «ای» آغازی افزوده شده است. «شکوه» به معنی «شکایت» واژه‌ای جداگانه و معرّب از عربی «شَکْوة» است و به این ریشه ربطی ندارد. ادعای نورایی و هر دو ارجاع او درست‌اند.

nodes.derivation: Sanskrit kaví- m. 'wise man, sage, seer, prophet; singer, bard, poet', adj. 'gifted with insight, intelligent, wise', is the Indic twin of Av. kauui-, both from Proto-Indo-Iranian *káwHiš, an -i- stem to PIE *(s)kewh₁- 'to perceive': the root's laryngeal survives as the Vedic hiatus/length in derivatives (kāvyá-), and the meaning is the concrete agent noun 'the one who perceives'. Pokorny p.587 and Horn p.196 both cite it in exactly this shape. The one point that overstates the evidence is Nourai's second gloss 'sovereign': that sense belongs only to the Iranian branch (and there only from the Younger Avesta on); no Sanskrit dictionary gives kaví- the meaning 'king'. Formally, too, the accepted lemma is kaví- (short i), not the kavî of the chart.

nodes.derivation: Avestan čəuuīšī is the 1st singular middle sigmatic aorist of the verb kav-/čav- 'to look out for, expect', translated by Bartholomae 'ich erhoffte, versah mich' ('I hoped, I expected'), i.e. exactly Nourai's 'attend, expect, hope'. The initial č- is the regular Iranian palatalisation of *k- before the front vowel of the s-aorist stem *kau-i-š- (the same alternation as Av. kav- : čəuu-), and -š- is the aorist marker; the form is attested once and is discussed by Bartholomae, BB 13.66 and AiW col. 442. It stands beside Skt. ā-kūvate 'intends' as the verbal use of the root. Note that the node's word is an inflected form, not a lemma, because Nourai copies it straight out of the two references he cites, both of which print it in exactly this shape.

nodes.derivation: There is no Old Persian word of this shape, and Old Persian has no infinitive in -twei. The form comes straight from the page Nourai cites: Pokorny p.588, last line of the s- section, reads 'apr. au-schaudītwei „vertrauen“', where 'apr.' is Pokorny's abbreviation for altpreußisch = OLD PRUSSIAN, a West Baltic language, not Old Persian (Pokorny's abbreviation for that is 'ap.'). Walde-Pokorny I 370 gives the fuller statement: 'Dasselbe d wie čudo scheint im s-anl. apr. au-schaudītwei „vertrauen“, auschaude „er traut“ vorzuliegen (Trautmann Apr. 308)'. The word is thus Old Prussian au-schaudī-twei, a prefixed (au- 'off, away') stative to the d-extension *(s)keud- of the root, with the Baltic infinitive suffix -twei, and it belongs to the same d-extension as OCS čudo 'wonder' and Gk. κῦδος. The mistake is Nourai's own — the printed page (image saved as data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/263.png) reads 'Old Persian' — so the extraction is faithful and the JSON needs no change; the entry is simply attached to the wrong branch of Indo-European. Aryanpur, working from the same Pokorny page, labels the identical form correctly as OLD PRUSSIAN.

nodes.derivation: The second word is right: Greek κῦδος kūdos 'glory, fame (esp. in battle)', Homeric and frequent in the Iliad, literally 'that which is heard of', is a neuter s-stem *kūd-os to the d-extension *keud-/*kūd- of this root, ablauting with OCS čudo 'wonder' — Pokorny prints 'd-Erweiterung keud- : kūd-os „Ruhm“' and Klein glosses it 'lit. means „that which is heard of“'. (Beekes dissents, deriving κῦδος and Slavic *čudo from a separate *kewd-s- 'miraculous power'.) The first word, however, is not Greek: 'akavein' is a misprint for ἀκούειν akouein 'to hear', the form that stands in Nourai's own reference — Watkins/AHD keu-¹ has 'suffixed form *ə-kous-yo- in Greek akouein, to hear: ACOUSTIC'. Greek ἀκούω goes back to *ə-kous-yō, with copulative ἀ- (< *sm̥-, 'together, with') prefixed to the s-extension *kous- of the root, so the -ou- is the inherited o-grade diphthong and can never appear as -av-. The printed page (data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/263.png) shows 'akavein', so the error is the book's, not the extraction's; the JSON should be left as it stands.

nodes.derivation: French acoustique is a learned 17th-18th century formation on the Latinised Greek acousticus < ἀκουστικός 'pertaining to hearing', the verbal adjective of ἀκούειν; it is first used as a noun for the science of sound by Joseph Sauveur in 1701 ('j'ai donc cru qu'il y avoit une science supérieure à la musique, et je l'ai appelée Acoustique'), the sense in which it then spread to the other European languages. nodes.derivation: Persian آکوستیک ākustik 'acoustics' is a 20th-century European technical loan, taken with the French shape: the initial آ- renders French /a/ in an open first syllable as Persian long ā (as in آنتن antenne, آسفالت asphalte), -ou- gives Persian و /u/, and the French ending -ique is regularly rendered -یک -ik in the Persian scientific vocabulary built from French in the Dār al-Funūn and post-Reza-Shah period (کلاسیک, تکنیک, فیزیک, الکتریک). An English source would have given *اکوستیک with initial short a and a different stress. The chart's route Greek → French → Persian is therefore right; it is simply the Persian end of the same chain that produced English acoustic.

nodes.derivation: English acoustic (c.1600, 'pertaining to hearing or sound') is taken from French acoustique, itself from Latinised Greek akoustikos (Klein, Etymonline); Skeat marks it simply '(Gk.)'. English kudos entered much later, in 1799, as Oxford and Cambridge university slang for 'fame, renown, glory', a direct book-borrowing of Greek κῦδος; the familiar back-formed singular 'kudo' (1936) rests on mistaking the Greek -s for an English plural. Both words therefore reach English from Greek, exactly as the chart's arrow says — with the qualification that acoustic came by way of French (which is why Nourai's own chart puts a French box in the parallel Persian line).

nodes.derivation: Latin caveō, cavēre 'to be on one's guard, take heed, beware' is a stative/denominative in -ē- built on the o-grade noun *kouos 'watchful' (Pokorny: 'lat. caveō, -ēre „sich in acht nehmen, sich vorsehen“ (*covēre, Denom. von *kouos)'), the same *kouos that underlies Greek κοέω 'I mark, perceive' — intervocalic *-ow- gives Latin -av-, hence cavēre beside the participle cautus (< *kaw-i-tos) and umbr. kutef. Watkins files it under keuə-¹ '1. Suffixed o-grade form *kous-o- becoming *kaw- in denominative (stative) Latin cavēre, to beware'. The gloss 'to watch' is a shade concrete for a verb whose Latin sense is 'to be wary, guard against', but the connection to the root's basic 'watch, pay attention' is exactly what the sources give. The book prints the vowel as cavěre with a breve; the Latin second-conjugation infinitive is cavēre with a long ē — a diacritic slip in the book, not a wrong word, and the extraction reproduces the page correctly.

nodes.derivation: The second word is right: Proto-Germanic *skauwōn 'to look at' (Old Saxon skauwōn, Old High German scouwōn, Old English scēawian, Gothic in us-skaws 'circumspect') from the s-mobile variant *skou- of the root — Nourai's 'skauuon' is simply the OS/PGmc form with uu for w, and both AHD ('Germanic *skauwōn in Old English scēawian, to look at: SHOW') and Pokorny print it in that shape. The first word is a misprint: the Germanic verb 'to hear' is *hauzjan-, attested as Gothic hausjan, ON heyra, OE hīeran, OS hōrian, OHG hōr(r)en, from the s-extension *kous- of the root with Verner's-law voicing of the *s. There is no Germanic *haujjan; the -jj- has arisen in the book by dropping the -s- and doubling the glide. AHD, the node's own reference, prints 'Germanic *hausjan'. The printed page (data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/263.png) reads 'haujjan', so the fault is the book's and the extraction is faithful. A second, milder point: 'Germanic' here means Proto-Germanic reconstructions, not an attested language, and skauuon is quoted in its Old Saxon shape.

nodes.derivation: hear < Middle English heren < Old English hīeran (West Saxon) / hēran (Anglian) < Proto-Germanic *hauzjan- (Gothic hausjan) < *kous-, the s-extension of the root; the OE verb already covered 'listen to, obey, follow, judge' as well as 'perceive by ear', and the modern spelling was separated from here between 1200 and 1550. show < Middle English sheuen < Old English scēawian 'to look at, see, gaze, behold' < Proto-Germanic *skauwōjan- < the s-mobile variant *skou-; around 1200 English alone turned the verb causative, 'let be seen, put in sight', and this displaced the older 'look at' within a century — which is why Nourai's Germanic gloss 'to look, show' carries both senses. The pair thus preserves in one modern language the two extensions (*kous- 'hear', *skou- 'see') that the root box heads.
